newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Glaxo Zantac under fire as rivals set truce.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Glaxo Zantac under fire as rivals set truce.

text.p: The final shots in a six-year battle to sell a generic version of top-selling ulcer drug Zantac may have been fired on Monday after two of the combatants signed a peace deal.

Canadian drug maker Novopharm Ltd said cheaper generic versions of the blockbuster drug, invented by Britain's Glaxo Wellcome Plc, had gone on immediate sale in parts of the U.S. after an agreement with rival manufacturer Genpharm.

The agreement followed years of legal wrangling between Glaxo and a clutch of companies eager to start selling versions of the drug in the U.S, which swallowed $1.6 billion worth of the ulcer tablets last year alone.
"I'm relieved. We have been fighting for this for six years," Novopharm chairman and chief executive officer Leslie Dan told Reuters.
Dan was hoping that Monday's accord ended an impasse which has kept all competitors off U.S. pharmacy shelves following the expiry of Glaxo's patent on Zantac on July 25.

Genpharm, which had temporarily been given exclusive rights to sell a generic competitor in the U.S. by the powerful U.S. Food and Drug Administration, couldn't actually make the product because of a patent dispute with Glaxo.

Novopharm, which had piled up stocks of tablets and paid Glaxo $70 million to be allowed to sell them two weeks before the patent officially expired, was stymied by a legal challenge from a third would-be competitor, Swiss-owned Geneva Pharmaceuticals Inc.
"We were in a difficult position where we had the product and Genpharm had the exclusive licence but no product because they were in litigation with Glaxo Wellcome," said Dan.

The two companies finally got together, with Genpharm passing on its right to market the drug to Novopharm in return for a share of the profits. Genpharm will give Novopharm a free run until the end of the year, when it expects to have its own pills ready for battle.
Novopharm is hoping to gain an advantage by flooding the market before anyone else can get in.

Dan told Reuters he planned to undercut Glaxo's Zantac price by 30 to 35 percent in the first few weeks and garner sales of "at least" $150 million to $175 million in the first month, helping recoup the wasted $70 million paid to Glaxo and the slice to be given to Genpharm.

But industry sources told Reuters there was still a danger the litigious Geneva, owned by the world's biggest drug company Novartis AG, would fight back with a further challenge. Geneva believes it has a stronger right to marketing exclusivity than Genpharm, part of Germany's Merck KGgA.

And even when the current round of civil war has subsided, analysts said the marketing battle for Zantac, also known as ranitidine hydrochloride, will become ever more cut-throat as new competitors queue up to join in.

Glaxo, quietly delighted by the squabbling among its would-be rivals which allowed it to carry on notching up $5 million of U.S. Zantac sales every day, was staying coolly above the fray on Monday. It has pumped the huge profits from Zantac, the world's best-selling drug for 11 years in a row, into developing a pipeline of products which it hopes will fill the big hole that competition will leave in its balance sheet.
